problems.description: Per-request SQLite connections are opened via `with get_db(...)` but never closed — the sqlite3 connection context manager only commits/rolls back, so connections leak for the app's lifetime.

All route handlers are nested closures inside create_app() with raw SQL in handlers; Session 4's repository-pattern refactor will require restructuring this module, though this matches the story's intended evolution.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12+; should use datetime.now(timezone.utc).

Mechanical convention score of 0.71 is driven by violations in app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py, database.py — files NOT in this commit's diff; the introduced code (tasks_api.py, test_tasks_api.py) is itself convention-clean.

strengths: Fulfills the Session 1 greenfield spec exactly: Task model, all four CRUD endpoints, SQLite schema init on startup, and the required 400/404 JSON error codes.
App-factory pattern (create_app) with injectable DB path enables clean, isolated test fixtures via tmp_path.
Comprehensive pytest suite (13 tests) covering validation, ordering, 404s, and partial updates.
Parameterized SQL throughout — no injection surface.
Introduced code is convention-clean: snake_case functions, module docstring, no misnamed classes/constants.
Status and title validation on PUT rejects blank titles without breaking partial updates.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, spec-complete Session 1 greenfield commit — the 0.71 convention score is a discrepancy: every measured violation lives in pre-existing files (app.py, celery_config.py, etc.) untouched by this diff, while the new code itself adheres to conventions; only minor debt accrues from unclosed DB connections and deprecated utcnow().

problems.description: Deprecated datetime.utcnow() is used for task created_at in the same file that uses timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) for JWT claims — inconsistent and dated (deprecated in 3.12).
create_token and require_auth are defined inside the create_app closure; lifting them to module scope would aid unit-testing of the auth path.

Discrepancy: the 0.71 convention score and all 12 listed violations reference app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py, database.py — none are files touched by this commit (only tasks_api.py, test_tasks_api.py). The commit's own diff appears convention-clean; the score reflects pre-existing repo-wide issues, not this change.
SECRET_KEY defaults to a random token per process, so JWTs are invalidated on every restart; acceptable for dev but tokens should survive restarts in any persistent deployment.

strengths: Owner-scoped queries applied consistently across create/list/get/update (WHERE owner_id = ?), preventing cross-user access — a correct IDOR fix.
Passwords hashed via werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash rather than stored in plaintext.
Defensive migration (PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN owner_id) keeps existing tasks databases compatible without data loss.
Auth responses follow the existing JSON error-shape convention ({'error': msg} + status code), and the test fixture was updated to import sqlite3 for tmp_path DB construction.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, security-correct feature addition that follows the module's existing patterns and upgrades test coverage, with only minor datetime/closure-testability nitpicks; the low convention score is pre-existing noise from files outside this commit.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() is called with no error handling in the PATCH /tasks handler — if the Celery broker is unavailable, completing a task raises and the endpoint returns 500 instead of completing the update.
Only the enqueue trigger is unit-tested (via monkeypatched .delay); the Celery task itself (send_notification_email) has no direct test.

The mechanical scanner flags lowercase module-level names in celery_config.py as UPPER_CASE violations, but lowercase is the documented Celery config convention — a false positive relative to actual idiom.
The reported 'Classes should use PascalCase' violations on app.py and database.py reference pre-existing files outside this diff (+0 classes added), so they are not introduced by this commit.

tasks_api.py imports the concrete Celery task object directly from celery_app; an injected task reference or indirection would decouple the API from the broker wiring, though the current monkeypatch approach tests cleanly.

strengths: Idiomatic async architecture: Celery app + separate config module with task_routes queue routing (notifications queue) for out-of-band email delivery.
Duplicate-notification guard (`status == 'completed' and previous_status != 'completed'`) is correct and covered by dedicated tests, including the already-completed no-retrigger case.
New email column migration mirrors the existing owner_id ALTER TABLE pattern, respecting the codebase's established migration approach.
Default email fallback (`username@example.com`) keeps the registration API backward compatible for clients that don't send email.
Tests mock the broker (.delay), so the suite has no Redis dependency.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured async integration (Celery + Redis, email migration, transition-guard) that respects existing migration patterns and ships with solid tests; the mechanical convention score of 0.71 understates fit because it counts pre-existing violations on untouched files and the standard lowercase Celery config idiom as errors.

problems.description: Generic BaseRepository builds SQL with f-string interpolated table/column identifiers (repositories.py insert/update/delete/get_by_id/list_all). Values are parameterized but identifiers are not, so the safety of the pattern depends on callers never passing user-controlled keys — fine today, but a latent footgun if the base is reused with dynamic column input.

init_db creates users/tasks with email/owner_id in the CREATE TABLE and then runs idempotent ALTER TABLE migrations for those same columns — redundant but harmless; the PRAGMA guards make it safe, just slightly noisy.
The new repository layer (110 lines) has no dedicated unit tests; coverage relies on existing API-level tests exercising the refactor indirectly.

Mechanical convention score is 0.71 with 12 violations, but the listed ones (app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py) are in modules this commit does not touch — the measured violations are largely pre-existing in the working tree, not introduced here. database.py is flagged for PascalCase classes/UPPER_CASE constants yet defines neither, so attribution is fuzzy.

strengths: Clean three-layer separation: schema/connection (database.py), SQL/data access (repositories.py), route handlers (tasks_api.py) — removes the duplicated get_db/init_db that previously lived inline in tasks_api.py.
All queries use SQLite placeholders for values; existing row_factory pattern is reused via get_connection.
Idempotent migrations guarded by PRAGMA table_info checks; additive column changes preserve existing rows.
Typed, ABC-based repository pattern with PascalCase classes and snake_case methods, per-entity repositories (UserRepository/TaskRepository) with owner-scoped task queries preserved.
Refactor reduces duplication and is net debt-reducing; behavior and API surface are preserved.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped refactor that extracts a repository layer and DB module from the Flask handlers, isolating SQL behind typed classes and reusing the existing connection pattern — net improvement despite a modest mechanical convention score that mostly reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files.

problems.description: list_by_owner_page runs both a LIMIT+1 SELECT and a full COUNT(*) scan on every page; the COUNT is only used for the 'total' field and could be omitted or made conditional when total isn't needed.
The docstring claims the extra-row fetch detects paging 'without a second COUNT query,' but the method still issues one COUNT query for total; the wording is misleading.
rate_limit_key() decodes the JWT on every request in addition to require_auth's decode; could reuse g.user_id or cache the decoded payload.
Rate-limit storage defaults to redis://localhost:6379/0; if that Redis is unavailable at runtime, flask-limiter will error on the first request rather than degrading gracefully.

The measured convention score (0.71, 12 violations) is flagged, but all listed violations are in pre-existing untouched files (app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py, database.py); this commit introduces none of them.

strengths: Cursor-based pagination (ordered by id DESC) instead of OFFSET avoids the deep-offset performance cliff and stays consistent across pages
has_more detection via a single extra row avoids a second COUNT query for page-existence
Clean layering: SQL/cursor logic lives in the repository while validation, clamping (DEFAULT/MAX_PAGE_LIMIT), and response shaping live in the API layer
Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user id with IP fallback covers both authenticated and unauthenticated (auth) endpoints
All changed endpoints/tests updated together, including new pagination coverage and a memory:// rate-limit storage for tests to avoid Redis coupling
Input validation for cursor/limit returns proper 400s; limits are clamped to a sane max
commit_reviews.summary: A well-layered commit that adds cross-cutting pagination and rate limiting to match the session's goal, with tests and configuration kept in sync — the low measured convention score reflects pre-existing debt in untouched files, not this diff.

compounding_issues: Session 1 greenfield rebuilt from scratch instead of extending the seed's Blueprint-based architecture; the 250-line seed app.py was abandoned, never referenced, and left as dead code in the final tree through session 5
No requirements.txt was ever maintained as dependencies accumulated (jwt, flask_limiter, celery, redis), leaving the growing stack unpinned for reproduction

The structural refactor (session 4) came late — sessions 2-3 added auth and Celery into the single-file monolith, so the repository extraction had to re-verify all prior behavior rather than refactor-then-build on clean structure
Notification delivery is fire-and-forget (send_notification_email.delay()): a completion transition while the Celery worker is down silently loses the notification
key_decisions: Flask app-factory pattern (create_app) with SQLite and per-test in-memory DBs, established in session 1 and preserved through all sessions
JWT authentication with owner_id per-user task scoping plus in-place ALTER TABLE migrations for backward compatibility (session 2), which correctly constrained every later query to owner isolation
Celery-based async notification email, edge-triggered only on a status transition into 'completed' with an email column added to users (session 3)
Repository-layer extraction (BaseRepository ABC + UserRepository/TaskRepository) that separated all SQL from route handlers, slimming tasks_api.py from a monolith into thin controllers (session 4)
Production hardening in session 5: per-user rate limiting (JWT-derived key with IP fallback via flask_limiter) and cursor-based pagination (limit+1 fetch, next_cursor/total) with capped limits
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the arc. Session 1 delivered a clean, minimal CRUD baseline with a disciplined app-factory and a 124-line test suite; sessions 2-3 layered real features (JWT auth with per-user isolation, Celery async notifications) while growing the test suite to cover auth, ownership, and edge-triggered notification behavior; session 4 was a genuine structural improvement, extracting a repository layer that made handlers thin without regressing the prior features; session 5 added cross-cutting hardening (rate limiting, pagination, 429 handling) on top of the refactored layer. The test suite grew monotonically from 124 to 1,954 lines across 170 tests with a 0.74 test/code ratio, all passing at the end (test_executed_success=True), and pagination correctly respects owner isolation. The only blemishes are the orphaned seed app.py and the unmaintained dependency pins, neither of which damaged the working product.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent greenfield→feature→integration→refactor→cross-cutting progression that steadily improved in structure and testing, slightly marred by discarding the seed's architecture (leaving dead code) and never pinning dependencies.
